📝 New article on Our World in Data: Around half of people will experience a mental health issue in their lifetime.

How many people struggle with mental health issues?

International and national health statistics will often give us estimates for how many people have depression, anxiety, or an eating disorder at any given time. But people can develop mental health disorders at any point in their lives, or experience recurring episodes over many years.

What share of people will ever experience one?

A study by John McGrath and colleagues tries to answer this question by drawing on data from 29 countries and over 150,000 people across the world. By interviewing people at different stages of life, they can build up an understanding of how this risk accumulates over an individual’s life course.

They estimate that roughly half of the population will experience one of 13 common mental health disorders by the time they reach 75.

Depression is the most common; by the age of 75, one in three women has experienced depression at some point in their lives. One in five men has.

For anxiety, the share is similar, as is the gender gap. For substance use disorders, it’s the opposite.

In this article, we look at these estimates in more detail and discuss why the true share might be even higher.

This week, many of the brightest minds in the field of fusion physics gather at an annual conference to discuss the remarkable physical process that lets us develop a new source of clean, abundant energy. At the event, Commonwealth Fusion Systems experts will bring a new subject of conversation: details about how we plan to operate SPARC, our fusion demonstration machine.

SPARC is about 80% complete. Its first job is to generate net fusion energy — called Q>1 in scientific circles. That means producing more power from the fusion process than it takes to heat up the fusion fuel, called a plasma, so that fusion occurs. It’s difficult, with only one machine in the world reaching this performance level. At CFS, we expect to be the second to reach Q>1, and we’ve begun detailed planning on the best way.

“Because SPARC is designed to run well beyond Q>1, we have lots of room to maneuver as we operate the machine,” said Clayton Myers, Interim Director of Diagnostics at CFS, who’s slated to discuss our Q>1 approach at the American Physical Society’s Division of Plasma Physics meeting (APS-DPP). “Part of the reason we’re confident SPARC will meet this early performance goal is because we have different paths to success.”

You can read more about our plans, including two options for magnetic field strength, in our blog post about APS-DPP. The link is in the comments below.

Among other talks and poster sessions at the conference, we’ll also share our newest work designing the ARC power plant, the successor to SPARC. And we'll have plenty of folks at our booth, so if you’re attending, stop by and say hello.

#FusionEnergy #SPARC

Solar and wind power have grown quickly in Poland, but coal still dominates.

The share of electricity produced by solar and wind in Poland more than doubled in just four years. In 2021, these renewable sources produced just 11% of its power; by 2025, this had risen to 25%.

You can see this growth in the chart, based on electricity data from Ember.

Solar and wind output, combined, grew very little in 2025, due to weak wind conditions. Solar output continued to grow, but it was barely enough to offset the decline in wind power.

Poland still has one of the most coal-intensive electricity mixes in Europe, with coal producing 50% of its power. The country has committed to moving away from it in the next few decades; growth in solar and wind generation will play a key role in this.

(written by @_HannahRitchie and @parriagadap)

Tohoku University and Toyota-supplier Aisin built a 16 nm AI chip (SoC) with 32 MB of embedded STT-MRAM that holds both a compact Linux boot image and Tiny YOLOv3 (object detection AI model) weights on-chip.

No external DRAM or SSD is needed for startup or inference. It boots in 65.7 milliseconds (39× faster) and runs object detection at ~50.7 mJ/frame with big energy savings. They used weight sharing and hybrid 8/16-bit math to fit the model. 

The chip also includes on-chip SRAM (used for feature maps and other working data) and a DDR interface, so external memory can still be attached when larger models or more capacity are needed. TSMC manufactures the chip.

Nice real-silicon demo of near-memory computing for edge AI — useful for automotive cameras, sensor fusion, and always-ready devices that need instant-on and low standby power. Not revolutionary: Others – Hailo, Ambarella, Renesas, etc. – already use large on-chip SRAM, embedded MRAM, or in-package DRAM, but it’s a good example of the gains when OS + model live in non-volatile on-chip memory. $TSM $AMBA #Hailo #Renesas #semiconductors

Revolut: Europe's most valuable startup ($200B) just showed the world its AI strategy.

Every company will end up copying it.

At the start of this year, Revolut leaned on the frontier labs. Its 2,000 engineers used Claude Code and Codex, and some burned $1,000 to $10,000 a month each. The bills kept climbing, and the returns weren't there.

So Revolut switched its default to an open-source model called GLM. All it needs is GPUs, which it rents from Together AI.

The results, by Revolut's own count:

- The bill is about a tenth of what it paid OpenAI and Anthropic
- Engineers get unlimited tokens instead of spending caps
- Coding time is down 60% and lead time is down 70%

That's the chart below.

Revolut still uses Claude and GPT, but only as "the exception," for the tasks they do best. Everything else runs on open source.

So here's the question I keep coming back to: how many use cases can companies really justify sending to frontier models?

My answer is very few. Plenty of companies still route everything to OpenAI and Anthropic today. For how long?

I think open source ends up handling the vast majority of corporate AI work, and frontier models get a short list of the hardest jobs. That's a problem for labs whose revenue forecasts assume unlimited growth.

If you appreciate unpopular takes, follow me @m0xt_ for more.

Yesterday the NYT published a list of what was alleged to be over 500 Michigan “Jewish leaders” supporting El-Sayed. The point of doing so was to paint a narrative that he has strong Jewish support in MI.

But did the NYT do any vetting to the list?

A quick skim and you notice it includes names like “Jack Mehoff”. I happen to know that one of the names is someone deceased. A majority of the signatories don’t even use their full names, just a last initial, so it’s impossible to confirm these are even real people or Jewish.

Why would they publish a story about a completely unreliable list with random names on a google sheet? Because the point was the narrative.
